items.q: **(Pressman / ISO 9126)** Which set lists ISO 9126 (product quality) characteristics?
options: Functionality, Reliability, Usability, Efficiency, Maintainability, Portability
items.explain: ISO 9126 defines six product-quality characteristics: Functionality, Reliability, Usability, Efficiency, Maintainability, Portability (ISO 25010 adds Security & Compatibility).

items.q: **(Pressman — function points)** The adjusted Function Point count is computed by multiplying the unadjusted count by a factor based on:
options: 14 general system characteristics (value adjustment / complexity factors)
items.explain: Pressman: FP = count-total × [0.65 + 0.01 × Σ(Fi)], where the Fi are 14 value-adjustment factors (general system characteristics) rated 0–5. The unadjusted count sums EI/EO/EQ/ILF/EIF × weights.

items.q: **(Pressman)** A key advantage of Function Points over Lines of Code as a size metric is that FP:
options: Is language-independent and can be estimated early from the requirements model
items.explain: Pressman: FP measures functionality delivered, so it is programming-language-independent and can be derived from the requirements/analysis model early, unlike LOC which is language-dependent and known late.

items.q: **(Pressman — white-box testing)** Which coverage criterion is the strongest of these, requiring each atomic condition to independently affect the decision outcome?
items.explain: Pressman: MC/DC (used in DO-178B/safety-critical avionics) is stronger than statement or branch coverage — every condition must be shown to independently affect the decision's outcome.

items.q: **(Pressman)** Basis path testing derives the number of independent paths to test from:
options: The cyclomatic complexity of the program's flow graph
items.explain: Pressman (McCabe): basis path testing uses cyclomatic complexity V(G) = E − N + 2 (or predicate nodes + 1) to determine the number of linearly independent paths — an upper bound on tests for branch coverage.

items.q: **(Pressman — testing strategy)** Validation testing succeeds when software functions in a manner that:
options: Can be reasonably expected by the customer (meets requirements)
items.explain: Pressman: validation testing succeeds when software functions in a manner that can be reasonably expected by the customer — assessed against the requirements (a Configuration review/audit accompanies it).

items.q: **(Pressman/Sommerville)** Alpha and beta testing differ in that beta testing is:
options: Conducted at the developer's site under controlled conditions
Conducted at end-user sites, 'live', without the developer present
items.explain: Alpha testing is at the developer's site with users in a controlled environment; beta testing is at end-user sites in the real (uncontrolled) environment, with users reporting problems back.

items.q: **(Pressman — system testing types)** Stress testing is designed to:
options: Execute the system in a manner that demands resources in abnormal quantity, frequency, or volume to find the breaking point
items.explain: Pressman: stress testing executes a system in a way that demands resources in abnormal quantity/frequency/volume — pushing it beyond design limits to observe failure behaviour. (Related: recovery, security, performance testing.)

items.q: **(Pressman — unit testing)** A 'driver' in unit/integration testing is a module that:
options: Replaces a superordinate (calling) module to invoke the unit under test
items.explain: Pressman: a driver is a 'main program' that accepts test data, passes it to the component, and prints results — replacing a calling (superordinate) module. A stub replaces a called (subordinate) module.

items.q: **(Pressman — integration)** A risk of 'big-bang' (non-incremental) integration is that:
options: When everything is combined at once, the many faults that surface are very hard to isolate and diagnose
items.explain: Pressman warns against big-bang integration: combining all components at once causes a chaotic set of errors that are extremely difficult to isolate; incremental integration is preferred.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch24 — metrics)** Sommerville distinguishes 'control metrics' from 'predictor metrics'. A predictor metric is one that:
options: Measures the management process (e.g. effort spent)
Is associated with the software product and helps predict its characteristics (e.g. cyclomatic complexity predicting maintainability)
items.explain: Sommerville Ch24: predictor metrics are product metrics (e.g. cyclomatic complexity, fan-in/fan-out, depth of inheritance) used to predict quality attributes like maintainability; control (process) metrics support management.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch24 — static product metrics)** Which is a static software product metric?
options: Cyclomatic complexity / fan-in–fan-out / depth of conditional nesting
items.explain: Sommerville Ch24 lists static metrics measured from the software itself: fan-in/fan-out, length of code, cyclomatic complexity, length of identifiers, depth of conditional nesting — these correlate with quality attributes.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch8 — release testing)** Sommerville notes release testing is usually a ___ testing process, derived from the system specification:
items.explain: Sommerville Ch8: release testing is a form of system testing, normally a black-box process where tests are derived from the system specification, to show the system delivers its specified functionality/performance/dependability.

items.q: **(Sommerville — security testing)** Risk-based security testing and penetration testing aim primarily to:
options: Identify vulnerabilities an attacker could exploit, by simulating attacks and probing the system's defenses
items.explain: Sommerville: security testing (including penetration testing) tries to find vulnerabilities by thinking like an attacker — identifying weaknesses that could be exploited, rather than just checking functional requirements.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch1 / ACM-IEEE Code)** Which is a principle of the ACM/IEEE-CS Software Engineering Code of Ethics?
options: Act consistently with the public interest; produce products that meet the highest professional standards
items.explain: The ACM/IEEE-CS code's eight principles include PUBLIC (act in the public interest), CLIENT/EMPLOYER, PRODUCT (high standards), JUDGMENT, MANAGEMENT, PROFESSION, COLLEAGUES, and SELF. Sommerville Ch1 echoes these professional responsibilities.

items.q: **(Sommerville Ch1 — professional responsibility)** An engineer who writes code to deceive regulators (e.g. an emissions defeat device) primarily violates which professional responsibility?
options: Acting with integrity / in the public interest (not misusing skills to harm society)
items.explain: Sommerville Ch1: software engineers must behave honestly and act in the public interest — deliberately deceiving regulators and harming the public (VW emissions) violates integrity and the duty to the public.

items.q: **(Sommerville — software reuse/licensing)** Why do companies typically vet or avoid GPL-licensed components in proprietary products?
options: GPL is copyleft — linking it can require the whole derivative product to be released under the GPL
items.explain: The GPL's copyleft ('viral') nature can force a derivative work that incorporates GPL code to be licensed under the GPL too — so companies vet third-party dependencies to avoid being forced to open-source proprietary code.

items.q: **(Goodhart / measurement theory)** Mandating '100% code coverage' as a hard target often backfires because:
options: When the measure becomes a target, developers write meaningless tests that hit lines without verifying behaviour
items.explain: Goodhart's law in practice: making coverage a mandatory target incentivizes gaming — developers write tests that execute code (raising the number) without meaningful assertions, so bugs still slip through.

items.q: **(Privacy engineering — data minimization)** Pseudonymization and anonymization are techniques that support which privacy principle?
options: Data minimization — reducing the personal data held/identifiable
items.explain: Data minimization reduces the amount and identifiability of personal data via de-identification, pseudonymization and anonymization — a core privacy-engineering mechanism aligned with GDPR/Privacy-by-Design.

items.q: **(Security testing — fuzzing)** Fuzzing is classified as a ___ analysis technique because it:
options: static; reads source without running it
dynamic; runs the program on many generated inputs and watches for crashes/faults
manual; requires human inspection of each input
items.explain: Fuzzing is a dynamic analysis technique: it executes the target program on large numbers of generated (random/malformed) inputs and monitors for crashes, memory errors, or assertion failures.
